en: *Continuation of the Catalogue of the Buddhist Scriptures of the Great Tang*, Volume One, with Preface. Begun at Ximing Monastery in the first year of the Linqi era and completed by Shi [Shi]shi at Zongchi Monastery.

Preface to the *Continuation of the Catalogue of the Buddhist Scriptures of the Great Tang*: If one rectifies the names of the Dharma, it is because of the profound sincerity of those who revere the jewels of the teaching.

This is truly the ocean of the ford for the common people’s access to the Dharma, and the lofty and vast height of the Sages. As time has passed, the principles remain as constant as the sun and moon in their majesty, regardless of status or rank.

How could one who preserves the magnificent beauty of the Way not regard the "trap and snare" of the inverted view of fortune as the precious position for a person of humble birth? From the time he announced his completion [of practice] in the Immortal Garden, he manifested the name of Pure Salvation (Jingji) to transform the multitudes; with his own hands he expounded the dust-like delusions, preaching according to their capacities and conditions, and manifesting the teachings through their inherent dispositions and desires. His net of instruction was cast once and for all, encompassing the great chiliocosm; such are those who receive his Way.
General Table of Contents for the Supplementary Section on the Translation of Various Scriptures in Successive Dynasties, Recorded According to Their Proximity, Part One, Volume One.

Regarding the scriptures translated in successive dynasties and the works composed by individuals: as these are all universally Dharma and are included within the category of scripture, they follow the emergence of the scriptures.
Supplementary Record of Translations from Successive Dynasties, Single and Multiple, with Biographies of Individuals and Records of Lost Works, Part Two, Volume Seven, refers to the aforementioned.

Later, as different individuals emerged and successive generations changed, the distinction between the monastic and the laity became further confused, and [the texts] were scattered in all directions. Now, having compiled and verified them in their entirety, there are both repeated and single accounts;

thus, one cannot know how the transmission was lost or how the succession continued. The third part of the *Zongce ru zang lu* (General Compendium of Works Included in the Canon), concerning the section on the Sūtras, is because the number of sūtras is vast.
Whether they are essential or exhaustive, they are listed in full. From the bundles, they are included in the canon according to their categories; therefore, they are divided into major sections.

The Fourth Volume of the *Xiaoxùdài zhòngjīng jùyào sòngshuō lù* (Record of Essential Recitations and Explanations of Various Sutras from the Later Successive Periods) refers to those works that, while seeking out essentials, were not overly verbose in their phrasing and meaning;

they were compiled according to their respective sections at appropriate times, though some remain incomplete. The Fifth Volume of the Record refers to those works whose titles appear across various catalogs but for which the original texts are missing;
it consists of a comprehensive inspection of all existing records to verify their definitive versions, excluding those that have been separately produced in different regions.
Section Six: A Record of Commentaries Composed by Monastics and Laypeople in Successive Generations, Not Yet Individually Identified as Preventing [Further Confusion].

This refers to commentaries on the words of former sages composed to enlighten those who have not yet awakened; where such works were previously titled as "Continued Records" (Xùlù), they are now separately cataloged here. Section Seven:

A Record of the Branch Streams of Various Scriptures Produced in Successive Generations and Their Dissemination. This refers to scriptures that arose independently and were not translated [into Chinese], which are here continued [in this record].

The Translation of the Extensive Texts and the Supplement for Beginners: All Verses Are Not to Be Disregarded. The Eighth Record: A Catalogue of Suspected and Spurious Sūtras and Śāstras Appearing Successively in Later Generations.

It is said that because the True Dharma is profound and remote, the ignorant and foolish have not yet attained realization; thus, in order to transform them according to worldly customs, there have been instances of interference with the authentic scriptures.
This record is therefore continued here. The Ninth: The Preface to the Complete Beginning and End of the Catalogue of Various Scriptures of Later Generations.

This refers to the fact that the previous catalogs did not exhaustively record the continuations of these scriptures. This tenth volume, titled *The Record of Miraculous Responses and Aroused Reverence for the Various Scriptures of Successive Dynasties*, records how, within the land of Dongxia (China), there were miraculous responses and auspicious signs through which beings received blessings and their faith was increased; it is for this reason that this record is appended.

It continues the *Record of the Translation Sources of the Various Scriptures of Successive Dynasties* and follows the *Great Tang Catalogue of Buddhist Scriptures*. It records the various scriptures of successive dynasties.
The first part of the *Lù* (Records) concerning the origins of translation begins with a brief account of the transmission of sounds;
thereafter, the profound and the simple followed by refining their methods to establish the foundations of their systems,
while enlightened sovereigns esteemed their principles and standards.
The sentiment lies in supervision;
the sovereign follows its natural order,
merely acting in accordance with it.
Thus, from the Later Han dynasty down to the Tang,
despite the changes in the world’s customs from refinement to decadence, the fundamental principles remained undivided;
all alike revered and upheld the supreme teachings.
It serves as the primary sign for extinguishing the fetters;
it embodies and understands the profound diagrams,
and acts as a mirror reflecting the fundamental basis of birth and death.
Thus, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* has been transmitted through successive generations, flourishing ever more brightly.
This is precisely because the flow of Dharma-giving has never ceased from moment to moment.
Now, in the Five Indias and the Western Regions (Tibet), the patriarchs have long revered the Celestial Words (the Vedic scriptures).
In the nine provinces of the Eastern Land, one follows the tracks of the birds;
thus, the celestial script and the celestial language remain beyond the reach of thought throughout the realm bounded by the seas.
As for these eight structural principles and six literary styles, they have rarely been encountered in the land of Daxia since its inception;
thus, what was heard of old through successive translations has only now been seen here.
Now, as for national histories and the ritual classics,
their substance and form are presented alternately;
so it is with the words of the Buddha and secular texts.
Regarding the natural aptitude for the principles of terminology, how is this known?
It is because the Buddha’s dissemination of the teaching prioritizes the Way (the Path).
To open the mind, unravel the primal simplicity, resolve doubts, and eliminate stagnation;
it does not rely on literary ornamentation nor preserve scrolls and volumes.
Its intent lies in awakening the obscurity and clarifying the principles of human emotion and reason.
That his divine thoughts were so swift and nimble—
this is precisely how it was brought about.
Listen attentively, listen attentively!
Reflect upon this well;
I shall analyze and explain it for you.
These are the words of the Sage.
Excellent, excellent!
We wish to hear it with joy.
We only pray that the World-Honored One will analyze and explain it for us.
This is how one receives the Dharma.
When words are weighty, the meaning is naturally grasped; there is no need to worry about prolixity or entanglement.
One should discuss only the correct discourse and refrain from engaging in mere literary debate.
This is the original scripture.
Its translation followed local customs;
as it was transmitted according to popular custom, it has largely fallen into superficiality and error.
Much has been lost. Thus,
Dao’an’s treatise on the "Five Losses" is easy to follow,
while Yancong’s composition on the "Eight Inversions" is difficult to equal.
This is indeed the authentic testimony;
other mundane customs need not be mentioned further.
Now, I shall record those worthy and wise individuals who translated [the scriptures] during the reigns of those emperors.
Furthermore, to manifest the partiality and rivalry between the sovereign’s faith and lack of faith,
this is established as the first record.
Now, as for the eras of the Han, Jin, Sui, Tang, and Song dynasties:
The world was one in great harmony.
At the beginning of each year, the Dharma-gate under his rule was unified throughout the successive dynasties of Wei, Song, Qi, and Liang.
The land was divided and split apart;
both the Chinese and the barbarians participated in governance, and their respective traditions emerged in parallel.
As for the extensive dissemination of these teachings and the transformation of customs, they were unprecedented and surpassed all that had come before.
I have thus observed that their brilliance has been spread far and wide through successive generations;
I shall now compile them according to their respective eras and append the works composed by both monastics and laypeople at the end.
It is hoped that those who come after will behold them as if they were face-to-face.

In total, eighteen successive dynasties produced a combined total of two thousand one hundred eighty-one works in six thousand seven hundred twenty-three fascicles; of these, three hundred and six works are later translations of scriptures.

During the Later Han dynasty, twelve monastics and laypeople transmitted and translated scriptures, vinayas, and other texts, producing four hundred and fifty-six works in four hundred and fifteen fascicles.
Subsequent translations comprised one hundred and twenty-five works, totaling one hundred and fifty-two new fascicles.
Following this, eight monks transmitted and translated during the Wei dynasty, continuing the work on scriptures and vinayas in one [fascicle].
Eleven works in twenty-seven fascicles were translated and transmitted by the Southern Tang’s family of Sūns;

eleven monastics and laypeople continued to produce one hundred twenty-two works in one hundred seventy-five fascicles, including further translations of sūtras and commentaries; one hundred five works in two hundred seventy fascicles were subsequently translated;
and during the Western Jin dynasty, nine monastics and laypeople are recorded as having translated and transmitted [the teachings], with subsequent translations following.
Three hundred and fifty scriptures and vinayas totaling seven hundred and fifteen fascicles;
ten supplementary translated scriptures totaling fifteen fascicles, translated during the Former Qin Fu dynasty; eight monks who transmitted the vinaya;
fifty supplementary scriptural catalogs totaling three hundred and twenty fascicles; and two monks who transmitted and translated during the Qin Qifu dynasty—the scriptures produced by them.
Twelve divisions and twenty-seven fascicles; eight additional translated scriptures totaling fifteen fascicles, transmitted and translated during the Former Liang Zhang dynasty by nine monks;

two hundred scriptures and vinaya texts totaling nine hundred and fifty fascicles produced by eleven monastics and laypeople during the Southern Liang Han Meng dynasty, including fifty-two scriptural transmissions totaling two hundred and seventy fascicles.
Continuation of the Translation of Scriptures, Five Sections, Eighteen Volumes. Translated by thirty-one monastics and laypersons during the Song Dynasty;
three hundred and twenty works totaling five hundred and forty volumes were subsequently produced.
During the Qi Dynasty, thirty monastics and laypersons produced sixty works totaling four hundred and twenty volumes on the Sūtras and Vinaya. During the Liang Dynasty...
Twenty-five monastics and laypeople translated eighty-seven works in nine hundred and two fascicles, including sutras, vinayas, and biographies, during the Yuan dynasty of the Later Wei.

Fourteen monastics and laypeople produced seventy-nine works in three hundred and sixty-eight fascicles, including sutras, vinayas, and biographies, during the [reign of] the Yuan family of the Later Wei.
Three monastics and laypeople translated [works] during the Gao family of the Later Qi.
Translated scriptures and treatises: nine divisions totaling forty-eight fascicles, translated by twenty monastics and laypersons during the Northern Zhou dynasty of the Yuwen clan;
scriptures, treatises, and works on astronomy, etc., twenty-five divisions totaling two hundred fascicles;

and scriptures, treatises, biographies, and commentaries, sixty divisions totaling two hundred and seventy fascicles, translated by five monastics and laypersons during the Chen dynasty; and [those from] the Sui dynasty.
A total of thirty-one individuals, including both monastics and laypeople, translated one hundred and seventy scriptures and treatises comprising seven hundred fascicles.

Furthermore, eighteen monastics of the Imperial Court jointly translated one hundred and twenty scriptures and treatises comprising one thousand seven hundred and twenty-one fascicles. Thus, the Buddha’s teachings were spread throughout the land of China.
Time has shifted through nine dynasties;
the court has distinguished between the true and the false, and the land has been interspersed with both Chinese and barbarians.
Consequently, the territories of the Five Liang, Four Yan, Three Qin, Two Zhao, Xia, and Shu were all situated in narrow and remote locations.
During the Jin and Song dynasties, as they held control over Jiangyin,
the Sūtra section of the canon was translated and transmitted, emerging according to local needs;
the aforementioned list includes those nations that were both comprehensive and orthodox.
I have recorded the origins of their transmission and translation;
as for the rest, I have not mentioned them,
because they lack universal applicability.
It is hoped that future readers will understand how this was achieved.

This concludes the *Continuation of the Record of Buddhist Scriptures of the Great Tang*, specifically the section on the one fascicle of scriptures brought by the Śramaṇa Kāśyapa Mātanga of the Later Han dynasty.

The monk Zhu Falan translated four works totaling eighteen fascicles; the śramaṇa An Qing (style name Shigao) translated one hundred and seventy-eight works totaling one hundred and ninety-seven fascicles;
the śramaṇa Lokakṣema translated twenty-one works totaling sixty-three fascicles;
the lay official and upāsaka An Xuan translated two works totaling three fascicles of sūtras; and the śramaṇa Zhu Foshuo [translated as follows].
One *sūtra* in two sections and three fascicles by the śramaṇa Zhi Yao; one *sūtra* in thirteen fascicles by the śramaṇa Kang Ju;
one *sūtra* in one fascicle by the lay devotee Yan Fotiao; seven *sūtras* in nine fascicles by the śramaṇa Kang Mengxiang;
six *sūtras* in nine [fascicles] by the śramaṇa Shi Tanguo; and one *sūtra* in two fascicles by the śramaṇa Zhu Dalü.
The second division consists of one hundred and twenty-five works in one hundred and forty-eight fascicles translated by various unknown translators, interspersed with incantations;
and the *Sūtra of Forty-two Sections*, one fascicle. Thus, there is one such work.
Translated during the reign of Emperor Ming of the Later Han dynasty by the Brahmin śramaṇa Kāśyapa Mātanga from Central India;
some also call him Zhu Shemoteng.
Various catalogs preserve [this record] with conflicting accounts; it is unclear which is correct.
Previously, it was not translated.
Therefore, I have recorded these matters in full.
In the tenth year of the Yongping era,
he returned eastward with the Han envoy Cai Yin and arrived at Luoyang.
This sutra was translated at the Baima Temple;
it has been compiled according to the catalog and is thus the patriarchal scripture of the land of Han.
The old catalog states:
"This sūtra is originally an excerpt from an Indian scripture;
it was initially produced by extracting and citing the essential points from a large compendium."
It resembles the eighteen chapters of the *Xiaojing*.
Dao’an’s catalog does not record it;
it appears in the old catalogs.
Furthermore, Sengyou’s *Collection of Records on the Translation of the Tripitaka* (*Chu Sanzang Jiji*), compiled during the reign of Emperor Shixing of the Han dynasty,
also records this; however, it notes that when the Great Dharma was first transmitted,
there were few who took refuge in it with faith, so Kāśyapa Mātanga retained his profound understanding and did not translate many more scriptures.
He later passed away in Luoyang.
The details of his life are recorded fully in Zhu Shixing’s biography.
As well as the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (*Gaoseng zhuan*), various miscellaneous records,
and so forth. The *Record of Baochang* (*Baochang lu*) states that those translated by Zhu Falan were [as follows].
These may have been recorded based on their arrival at the same time.

*The Sutra of the Buddha’s Past Deeds* (5 fascicles), *The Sutra on Severing Bonds in the Ten Stages* (4 fascicles, or 8 fascicles; see Zhu Shixing’s Catalogue), *The Combined Differences of the Two Hundred and Sixty Precepts* (2 fascicles; see the Separate Catalogue), *The Sutra of the Dharma-Ocean Treasury* (1 fascicle; one version lacks the character "zàng"), and *The Sutra of the Buddha’s Former Births* (1 fascicle). These constitute five works.
In total there are thirteen fascicles.
These were brought by the śramaṇa Dharmaratna from the kingdom of Central India, together with Kāśyapa Mātanga;
they traveled by different routes and arrived at different times.
It was translated during the reign of Emperor Ming.
Initially, he and Teng produced the *Sutra in Forty-two Sections*. After Teng passed away, [the work continued].
Translated by Lan herself.
Formerly, when Emperor Wu of Han dredged the bottom of Kunming Lake, he obtained ashes and ink.
He questioned Dongfang Shuo about them.
Shuo said, "This is not within my knowledge;
you may inquire of the Hu people from the Western Regions."
When Fali arrived,
he questioned Lan about this,
and Lan said:
"This is indeed the residual ash from the conflagration at the end of the kalpa.
Such was the testimony of Yue,
and those who believed him were very numerous.
Furthermore, when the envoy Qin Jing returned from the kingdom of Yuezhi,
he obtained a sandalwood image of King Udayana and a fourth model of a painted image;
these were brought to Luoyang.
The Emperor issued an edict to have it depicted.
It was enshrined for veneration at the Xiyang City Gate and atop the Xianjie Mausoleum;
from that time until the present, its colored and monochrome versions have been widely circulated.
Furthermore, as the Buddha-dharma first arrived and heterodox paths were in conflict and competition,
he subsequently recorded contemporary events and composed the *Hanfa benneizhuan* (Inner Biography of the Origin of the Dharma in Han) in five fascicles;
the author is not known with certainty.
It exists today. The *Xiuxing daodi jing* (Sūtra on the Stages of Cultivating the Path) consists of six fascicles; it appeared in Zhi Mindu’s catalogue and its preface was composed by him.

According to one entry in Baochang’s catalogue and the *Bielu*, the *Shun daoxing jing* (Sūtra on Following the Practice of the Path) and the *Dāseng weiyi jing* (Sūtra on the Great Monastic Discipline) consist of four fascicles and are listed as recently appended distinct translations in the *Bielu*.
The *Fayun jing* (Dharmapada-sūtra) in four fascicles, which is recorded separately as being identical to the *Weiyi jing* (Vinaya-vidhi-sūtra), is combined here [with it] by this separate catalog;
however, Sengyou’s catalog divides it into two sections in two fascicles. The *Xianxing san shiqi pin jing* (Saptatriṃśat-dhyāna-prasthāna-sūtra) in one fascicle appears in Baochang’s catalog.
The *Shibao fa jing* (Daśa-nidāna-sūtra) in two fascicles is noted in Sengyou’s catalog as either one fascicle or with many additional chapters.
The *Jiùlù* (Old Catalogue) states that the *Cháng āhán yīn chí rù jīng* (Dīrgha Āgama: Dhātuvibhaṅga Sūtra) in two fascicles was translated [by An Shigao];
the *Bièlù* (Separate Catalogue) states that Dao’an annotated it, as seen in Zhu Shixing’s *Hàn lù* and Sengyou’s *Lù*. The *Ān bān shǒuyì jīng* (Anāpāna-smṛti Sūtra) in two fascicles:
Dao’an stated it was the "Minor Ānāpāna," as seen in the records of Zhu Shixing, Sengyou, and Li Kuò. The *Ān bān jīng* (Ānāpāna Sūtra) in one fascicle: Dao’an [annotated it].

The commentary (note) appears in Sengyou’s *Chu sanzang jiji*, section on miscellaneous works, entry no. 44. It consists of two fascicles of scripture; some say it comprises forty-four sections, but as their titles are not clearly indicated, it is unknown which sūtras they are.
Dao’an stated that it was extracted from the *Ekottarika Āgama*. Sengyou’s catalogue records the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-bhūmi-sūtra* in two fascicles, for which Dao’an originally composed a commentary.
This is an excerpt from the *Xiuxing jing* (Sūtra on the Practice); there is no abbreviated Chinese version, or perhaps the large characters are missing.

*Chang ahan jian yu lu daoyi faxing jing* (The Sūtra on the Practice of the Will for Enlightenment from the *Dīrgha Āgama*), two fascicles; sometimes one fascicle in the *Dīrgha Āgama*. Recorded in the catalogs of Dao’an and Zhu Fahu.
*Chan jing* (Sūtra on Dhyāna), two fascicles; first appeared in the *Bie lu* (Separate Catalog). *Wuliangshou jing* (Sūtra of Immeasurable Life), two fascicles; first appeared in the *Bie lu*.
*Shamen Tanluan zhu lun jiezhao bailiu shipin jing* (The Treatise and Commentary by the Śramaṇa Tanluan on the Sūtra of One Hundred and Sixty Chapters), one fascicle.
The *Jiùlù* (Old Catalogue) states that the *Zēngyī Āhán Bǎilíngzhī Zhāngjīng* (Ekottarika-āgama, Sūtra in One Hundred and Sixty Chapters) is found in Sengyou’s catalogue under volume 12 of the *Dà*.

The *Bièlù* (Separate Catalogue) states that the *Shí’èr Ménjīng* (Sūtra of Twelve Gates) in one fascicle consists of two fascicles and is an excerpt from the *Cháng Āhán*; it is annotated by Dao’an and is found in both the *Chàng* and *Sengyōu* catalogues.

The *Xiǎo Shí’èr Ménjīng* in one fascicle is also an excerpt from the *Cháng Āhán*, as seen in both the *Chàng* and *Sengyōu* catalogues. The *Qīfǎ Jīng* (Sūtra of Seven Dharmas) in one fascicle is recorded in the old [catalogues].
The Catalogue states: The *Abhidharma Saptadharmapratipatti-sūtra* is found in the *Dīrghāgama*, or is simply called the *Saptadharmapratipatti*;
see Sengyou’s Catalogue. The *Caturdaśamati-sūtra*, one fascicle; the old catalogues call it the *Bodhisattvacaturdaśamati-sūtra*;
see Sengyou’s Catalogue. The *Abhidharmāṣṭanavati-saṃyojana-sūtra*, one fascicle; see Sengyou’s Catalogue. The *Prajñāpāramitāpañcāśatsaṃkhyāgaṇanā-sūtra*, two [fascicles].
*Jian yu lu*, one fascicle; *Nantika layavastu sūtra*, one fascicle (also known as *Dufu changzhe jing*, or alternatively *Dufu changzhe caiwu wufu jing*, or *Wuzi fuyu jing*);
from the *Za ahan*, fascicle 46, *Changzhe aonao erchu jing* (alternatively titled *Changzhe aonao jing*).
Regarding the *Dvayāśraya-sūtra*, one version is titled the *Dvayāśraya-vighāta-sūtra*; the following texts are all single fascicles:
the *Gṛhapati-kaukṛtya-pratikramaṇa-sūtra* (also known as the *Śreṇika-gṛhapati-kaukṛtya-buddha-pūjā-pratikramaṇa-sūtra*), the origin of which is Śreṇika, though it remains uncertain who he was;
and the *Indriya-paripāka-sūtra* preached by the Buddha for Nāku (one version says for the elder Nākulaputra).
The *Sūtra on the Elder Brothers Visiting the Buddha*—one version states that the two elder brothers, Liśāta and [his brother], went to the place where the Buddha was;

this sūtra appears in the *Madhyama Āgama*. The *Sūtra on the Buddha’s Supernatural Power Saving the Elder’s Son* and the *Sūtra on Anāthapiṇḍada Converting His Seven Sons* appear in the *Ekottara Āgama*.
The *Sūtra on the Layman Daśabala of Aṣṭaka* appears in the *Madhyama Āgama*, number [ ].
The Sūtra of the Licchavi Vimalakīrti’s Sixty Fearlessnesses, translated from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, fascicle 21;

The Sūtra of the Elder’s Receiving of the Blessing of the Dharma (also known as the *Sūtra of the Most Victorious Elder’s Receiving of the Blessing of the Dharma*); The Sūtra of the Elder’s Son Jīvaka (also known as the *Jīvaka Sūtra*);
The Sūtra of the Layman Ugga Seeing the Buddha and Hearing the Dharma and Attaining Enlightenment (also known as the *Sūtra of the Sugata Layman*).
*The Sūtra on Attaining Awakening through the Preaching of the Dharma*, translated from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. *The Sūtra on Attaining the Extraordinary Contemplation*.
*The Sūtra of the Elder Ekasāṭaka’s Nightly Exhortation*; first appearing in the old catalogs as one title.

Also known as *The Sūtra of Prince Śatavakana’s Explanation of the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions*. Also known as *The Sūtra of Prince Tiāngxīng (Venus) and the Twenty-eight Lunar Mansions*. Also known as *The Tiger*.

*Ear-jing chujia yinyuan jing* (The Scripture on the Causes and Conditions for Leaving Home Heard by the Ear), one fascicle; *Jiafo shuo zidan yun chujia yuan jing* (The Scripture Spoken by the Buddha on the Causes and Conditions for Leaving Home, with Characters Only);
*Fodu zhantuluo er chujia jing* (The Scripture on the Buddha Delivering a Caṇḍāla Boy to Leave Home); *Chuntuo shami jing* (The Scripture on the Śrāmaṇera Cunda), also written as *Shamen* (Śramaṇa);

these appear in the twenty-fourth fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. *Waidao chujia jing* (The Scripture on the Leaving Home of Non-Buddhists) and *Jingqin sinianchu jing* (The Scripture on Diligently Practicing the Four Foundations of Mindfulness) appear in the second fascicle of the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
Volume nineteen: *The Sūtra on the Difficulty of Repaying Parental Kindness* (also known as the *Sūtra on the Difficulty of Repaying*), translated from the *Madhyama Āgama*;

*The Sūtra on the Fulfillment of Dhyāna Contemplation*, translated from the *Āgama*; *The Sūtra on the Practice of Counting the Breath*, *The Sūtra on the Methods of Dhyāna*, and *The Secret Essentials of Dhyāna*.

[The latter] appears in the *Sūtra on the Secret Essentials of Dhyāna for Healing Illness*, though some versions omit the character "secret" (*mi*). *The Sūtra on Worldly Beautiful Colors*, translated from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. Volume twenty-four.
The *Sarvasaṃskārā anityāvasthita-sūtra* appears in the *Saṃyuktāgama*, fascicle 34; the *Puruṣakāya-skandhapraveśa-sūtra* appears in the first fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*;
the *Bahuviparyāsa-dṛṣṭi-sattva-sūtra* (lacking the character "duō" [many]) appears in the sixteenth fascicle of the *Udānavarga*;
and the *Caturcatvāriṃśad-roga-puruṣakāya-sūtra* appears in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.

Volume One: "The Human Sickness That the Physician Cannot Cure" (from the *Xiuxing Dizhi Jing*), "The Discernment of What Arises from Good and Evil" (*Fenbie Shan'e Suoqi Jing*), "Cutting the Poisonous Tree Yet It Grows Again" (*Zhuo Dushu Fusheng Jing*), "Extracted from the *Chuyao Jing*," "The Sequential Methods for the Expedient Means of Dhyāna-Samādhi" (*Chanding Fangbian Cidifa Jing*), "The Methods for Practicing Dhyāna in Araṇya" (*Alanye Xichanfa Jing*), "Extracted from the *Pusa Chanfa* [Chapter] One: The Names of the Four Hundred Samādhis. [End of Volume One] Part One: The First Four Hundred Samādhis. 1. The Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Unobstructed Wisdom; 2. The Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Unhindered Mind; 3. The Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Unimpeded Body; 4. The Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Unobstructed Eye; 5. The Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Unobstructed Ear; 6. The Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Unobstructed Nose; 7. The Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Unobstructed Tongue; 8. The Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Unobstructed Body; 9. The Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Unobstructed Mind; 10. The Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Unobstructed Wisdom. 11. The Samādhi of the Tathāgata’s Unobstructed Dharma-Eye; 12. The internal title of the *Śīlasamādhi Sūtra* states: "Chapter Four: Sole Realization," excerpted from the "Pure Conduct of Bhikṣus.
Its initial excerpt differs slightly from that found in the *Hushi* (Protecting the Teacher). The *Vaiḍūryarāja Sūtra* has its initial excerpt.

The *Zengyi Mamayi Jing* (Ekottarikāgama on the Meaning of Abuse) was spoken by the Buddha for the Brahmin Bimbisāra; it is excerpted from the eleventh fascicle of the *Saṃyuktāgama*, [specifically] the "Brahmin Inquiry."
*The Sūtra on the Blessings Attained through the Buddha’s Almsgiving*; *The Sūtra on the Buddha Preaching the Dharma for the Village Head of Aśvakarṇa*;
both from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, Volume 32. *The Sūtra on the Conduct of the Brāhmaṇa*; from the *Madhyama Āgama*, Volume 39.

*The Sūtra on the Brāhmaṇa Duṣika Discussing the Meaning and Leaving Home*; from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*. *The Sūtra on the Buddha Preaching the Dharma for the Fire-Worshipping Brāhmaṇa and His Realization of the Way*.
The *Brahmin Hypocrisy Sūtra* from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*; the thirty-fascicle *Saṃyukta Āgama*;
the *Sūtra on the Buddha’s Great Transformation of a Brahmin Who Left Home*, also known as the *Sūtra on the Buddha Explaining to Ajita Keśakambala that Suffering is Created by Oneself or Another*;
and the *Sūtra on the Death of a Brahmin Son Whose Affection Remained Unabated*, all from the *Ekottara Āgama*.
The *Cāturmahārāja-brāhmaṇa-pravrajyā-mārga-prāpti-sūtra* from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*; the *Gāthā-sūtra* spoken by the Buddha for the arrogant brāhmaṇa from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*;
the *Brāhmaṇa-śuklavāsas-sūtra* from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*; the *Brāhmaṇa-pṛcchati-bhaviṣya-kati-buddha-sūtra* from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*;
the *Brāhmaṇa-parihāra-maraṇa-sūtra* from the *Ekottarika Āgama*; and the [sūtra] spoken by the Buddha for a brāhmaṇa.
The *Kṛṣikārāma-sūtra* (Sūtra on Plowing the Field), from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*; the *Saptasthavira-brāhmaṇa-pratijñā-śiṣya-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Seven Elder Brāhmaṇas Requesting to be Disciples);

the *Brāhmaṇa-vidyā-vibhāga-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Brāhmaṇa Mastering the Treatises), from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*; the *Buddha-nagna-putra-āvaraṇa-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Buddha Covering the Naked Son); the *Jātaka-sūtra* (Birth Sūtra);

the *Brāhmaṇa-jñāna-sarva-kalā-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Brāhmaṇa Understanding All Arts), from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*; the *Buddha-brāhmaṇa-caturdharma-sūtra* (Sūtra on the Buddha Teaching the Four Dharmas to a Brāhmaṇa), from the *Saṃyukta Āgama*; [and] the Buddha.
For the sake of young Brahmins, he preached the *Sūtra on the Wholesome and Unwholesome*, the *Sūtra on Illusion-like Samādhi* (in two fascicles), the *Ānāpāna Sūtra*, and the *Antargarbha Sūtra*.
The latter was the second translation, made in the tenth month of the second year of the Yuanjia era;

it is also known as the *Antargarbha-śata-pada* or the *Śata-ratna*, and is recorded in Zhu Shixing’s *Han-lu*. Furthermore, the *Sūtra on the Methods for the Essentials of Five-Gate Dhyāna* first emerged from the water.
The *Yujing* (Sūtra of Similes) contains the *Zenghan Fumu Piyu Jing* (Sūtra of the Simile of the Floating Wood from the Ekottarika Āgama) and the *Bieyu Jing* (Sūtra of the Turtle).

The *Shijialuoyue Liuxiangbai Jing* (Sūtra of Śikhālāvatsa’s Sixfold Prostration), also known as the *Da Liuxiangbai Jing*, is included here.
